source.title: AI Cartography: Mapping the Latent Landscape of AI Benchmark Ecosystems
source.authors: Michael Hardy; Anka Reuel; Lijin Zhang; J. Casabianca; Sang T. Truong; Yash Dave; Han D. Lee; Benjamin Domingue; O. Koyejo

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests scaling relationships using observational leaderboard scores and latent benchmark abilities rather than controlled pretraining-loss measurements or compute sweeps.
record.gate_note: The paper tests downstream benchmark performance against parameter count and compares manifest-score and noise-controlled latent scaling estimates. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, vary training tokens or compute, test compute-optimal allocations, or test architecture shape at fixed parameter count. Statements about the original scaling-law studies and other cited work are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: An observational analysis of 4,281 Open LLM Leaderboard models that regresses downstream benchmark scores and latent abilities on log10 parameter count. That bears on V6 (downstream improvement with scale). It does not measure pretraining loss, tokens, compute, allocation or architecture shape at fixed size.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Authors conclude scaling is a vector of slopes over latent abilities, not one scalar law. The general factor scales strongly and stably with size, benchmark-specific residual factors vary (strong for MMLU-Pro; trivial or absent for GPQA, BBH and IF-Eval; slightly negative for MuSR). Manifest-score scaling slopes are unreliable (Rβ=0.53) without ecosystem controls.
record.recipe_differences: Uses observational Open LLM Leaderboard submissions, benchmark scores and latent-factor regression, rather than controlled pretraining runs measuring held-out loss across parameters, tokens and compute. It analyzes parameter-count associations and ecosystem heterogeneity, not compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling conclusion changes between manifest leaderboard scores and latent-factor estimates with ecosystem controls; benchmark-specific slopes also differ substantially across factors.

fits_no_version.finding: The estimated size slope on downstream scores depends on the measurement model. Manifest scores give Rβ=0.53 and CVβ=0.944, while latent g gives Rg=0.97. Benchmark identity accounts for 30% of slope instability (PSI).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream scaling slopes estimated from aggregate benchmark scores depend on the measurement model and ecosystem controls; they are not stable single laws.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The scaling evidence is observational and the authors caution against causal interpretation. It uses one leaderboard snapshot and six benchmarks; submissions are not representative of all LLMs, metadata are noisy proxies, and the authors describe ecosystem effects and benchmark-specific scaling as context-dependent. It does not test pretraining loss, tokens, compute budgets, or extrapolation to larger runs.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss; power-law form in parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating small-run fits to much larger runs.
Depth/width or other shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Prediction from pretraining loss; forecasting unseen larger models; controlled training runs (all evidence is cross-sectional across heterogeneous submissions).
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method; curvature away from a power law.

missing.what: Share of score variance linked to model size: Ωsize-all=0.402, Ωx=0.135, benchmark-demeaned Ωx=0.26.
Coefficient of variation of effective slopes (CVβ=0.944) and Benchmark PSI=0.30 as the largest source of slope instability.
Size scaling of latent scores broken down by deployment type (chat, domain-specific, merges, base, continued pretraining).

record.verdict_notes: I removed the V7 links. V7 concerns exponents and compute-optimal splits of pretraining-loss laws; this study's slope-reliability findings are about downstream scores and are recorded under fits_no_version. Benchmark-specific factors are orthogonal residuals after g, so their null slopes do not imply raw benchmark scores fail to scale; hence limits_scope rather than challenges for MuSR. The MuSR sign conflicts between prose (negative) and the flattened Table 3 (+0.04). All results are observational, linear in log10 params, and confounded by provenance, as the authors acknowledge.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss; power-law behavior in parameters, tokens, or compute; and the several-orders-of-magnitude range.
Forecasting the loss of much larger runs from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and how either quantity scales with a fixed compute budget.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count, including depth and width.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer as tests of the same power-law form.
The study reports size associations for downstream benchmark and latent-factor scores, not predictive accuracy of forecasts on unseen larger runs or prediction from pretraining loss.

It shows differences between manifest-score scaling and latent, ecosystem-controlled scaling, and heterogeneity across latent dimensions. It does not test compute-optimal splits, directly compare the original papers’ exponents, or establish that curves bend away from a power law. It does not manipulate training schedule or data.

rows.measure: Reliability and signal-to-noise of the average manifest-score scaling slope
rows.value: Rβ = 0.53; SNRβ = 1.12. The authors say an average scaling law would be misleading and scaling is context-dependent.
rows.note: This concerns leaderboard benchmark scores, not pretraining loss. The paper also reports a positive and significant average size effect in §J.1.1, but the slope reliability indicates substantial context dependence.
rows.check: Drop the V7 link. V7 concerns fitted exponents and compute-optimal splits of pretraining-loss laws; this row is about the reliability of a downstream-score slope. The average manifest slope is positive and significant (§J.1.1), but SNRβ=1.12 and Rβ=0.53 show it is highly context-dependent. The heterogeneity part belongs under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: General latent factor g and the MMLU-Pro-specific factor, with contributor and deployment controls
relationships.reason: g rises strongly and stably with log params (β=1.05, Rg=0.97), and the MMLU-specific factor also rises (β=0.52) (R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: The general factor increased strongly with log parameters at β=1.05 and R_g=0.97, while the MMLU-Pro-specific factor increased at β=0.52.

relationships.condition: Manifest leaderboard scores pooled across benchmarks and ecosystem facets
relationships.reason: The average size slope is positive, but SNRβ=1.12 and Rβ=0.53 mean context-specific slope variation rivals the mean slope (R1).
relationships.display_finding: The average size slope was positive, but SNRβ=1.12 and Rβ=0.53 indicated contextual variation comparable to the mean slope.

relationships.condition: Benchmark-specific residual factors (GPQA, BBH, IF-Eval, MATH L5, MuSR) after partialling g
relationships.reason: Residual slopes are trivial, non-significant or small and unreliable, and per the prose negative for MuSR. Gains on these benchmarks run through g rather than specific skills (R4–R8).
relationships.display_finding: After accounting for general ability, benchmark-specific slopes were negligible or unreliable and negative for MuSR, indicating gains primarily through general ability.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: General latent ability and the MMLU-Pro-specific factor
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports a strong, stable positive size relationship for g and a strong denoised size effect for MMLU-Pro (R2–R3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: BBH, GPQA and IF-Eval-specific factors after controls
reader_labels.reason: The BBH and GPQA size effects are described as trivial and the IF-Eval effect is not significant, so the relationship is not uniform across downstream factors (R4–R6).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The reported size relationship is small and significantly negative rather than improving with scale (R7).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Manifest-score versus latent-factor scaling, and benchmark-specific latent scaling
reader_labels.reason: Manifest-slope reliability is Rβ = 0.53, whereas general-factor reliability is Rg = 0.97; the benchmark-specific results also range from strong to negligible, absent or negative (R1–R7).
